title: Entangling Power Dynamics: Ergodicity and Mixing
authors: Rahul V, Ranjan Modak, Shaon Sahoo, S Aravinda
abstract: We study quantum dynamics through the lens of entanglement generation and characterize the underlying unitary evolution by the distinct signatures it imprints on the time-dependent entangling power. For a unitary operator, we characterize ergodicity by the equality between its long-time-averaged entangling power and the Haar-averaged linear entropy. We define mixing more stringently as the convergence of the time-dependent entangling power itself to the Haar value at long times. Within this framework, we establish the ergodic hierarchy of dynamical behavior, showing in particular that mixing implies ergodicity, whereas ergodicity does not necessarily imply mixing. As an application, we find that two-qubit unitary gates are neither ergodic nor mixing: their long-time-averaged entangling power can take only four discrete values, none of which coincides with the Haar average. We then investigate many-body dynamics using the kicked Ising chain and find that the long-time-averaged entangling power converges to the Haar value in both integrable and nonintegrable cases, indicating ergodicity. Remarkably, however, the nonintegrable chain exhibits mixing, whereas the integrable chain, despite being ergodic, is demonstrably nonmixing. We also introduce a Lyapunov-like exponent to characterize the rate at which the time-dependent entangling power approaches its saturation value. We find that this exponent increases systematically with the degree of integrability breaking in the many-body system. Our results establish entanglement generation as a useful framework for characterizing dynamical systems and reveal qualitatively different signatures of integrability beyond conventional diagnostics.
summary: This paper develops a framework using entangling power to diagnose quantum dynamics, establishing a hierarchy where mixing implies ergodicity, but not the reverse. By applying this to the kicked Ising chain, the authors successfully distinguish between ergodic (but nonmixing) and mixing systems, providing a powerful tool for classifying quantum chaotic behavior.
main_problem: The paper aims to characterize the underlying dynamics of quantum evolution by studying the signatures imprinted on the time-dependent entangling power, specifically distinguishing between ergodicity and mixing.
main_result: The authors establish that mixing implies ergodicity, but not vice versa; they show that nonintegrable many-body systems can exhibit mixing while integrable ones remain ergodic but nonmixing.
method: The analysis uses the entangling power, defined via linear entropy, to quantify entanglement generation over time. They introduce a Lyapunov-like exponent to characterize the rate of approach to saturation.
model_or_system: The study applies to general unitary operators, specifically analyzing two-qubit gates and the kicked Ising chain in both integrable and nonintegrable regimes.
key_observables: Entangling Power ($	ext{ep}(U)$), Long-time-averaged entangling power ($	ext{epsat}(U)$), Lyapunov-like exponent, and the Haar-averaged linear entropy.
important_parameters: Degree of integrability breaking ($\delta$), time steps ($n$), and the system size (for the Ising chain).
main_assumptions: The characterization relies on the definitions of ergodicity (average equals Haar average) and mixing (time-dependent power converges to Haar average).
figures_summary: Figures likely show the time evolution of entangling power for different parameters ($\delta$) and the systematic increase of the decay rate ($\lambda$) with the degree of integrability breaking.
paper_structure: The paper first defines the diagnostic tools (entangling power, ergodicity, mixing) and then applies them sequentially to two-qubit gates and the kicked Ising chain, culminating in the establishment of the ergodic hierarchy and the Lyapunov exponent analysis.
why_interesting: This work provides a novel, information-theoretic diagnostic tool (entangling power) to distinguish between different dynamical regimes (ergodic vs. mixing) in quantum many-body systems, offering insights beyond traditional spectral or correlation function analyses.
